reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ESC guidelines
clinicalPearls: A cardiomyopathy caused by chronic infection with the protozoan parasite Trypanosoma cruzi, transmitted mainly by triatomine bugs in endemic parts of Latin America
Most infected people remain in an indeterminate phase for years, and only a proportion later develop cardiac or gastrointestinal disease
Cardiac manifestations include conduction disease, ventricular arrhythmias, dilated cardiomyopathy with heart failure, and thromboembolism
Right bundle branch block combined with left anterior fascicular block is a characteristic ECG pattern
A left ventricular apical aneurysm is a notable feature and a site for mural thrombus formation and embolism
The disease should be considered in patients from endemic regions presenting with unexplained cardiomyopathy, heart block, or ventricular arrhythmia
Diagnosis of chronic infection rests on serological detection of antibodies to the parasite
Management combines antiparasitic therapy in appropriate patients with treatment of heart failure, arrhythmia, conduction disease, and thromboembolic risk
reference.pathophysiology: After initial infection with Trypanosoma cruzi, the parasite persists at low levels in tissues including the myocardium. Chronic Chagas cardiomyopathy is thought to result from a combination of low-grade persistent parasitism, immune-mediated and autoimmune myocardial injury, microvascular dysfunction, and damage to the cardiac autonomic nervous system. Progressive myocarditis and fibrosis disrupt the conduction system and create arrhythmic substrate, and lead to chamber dilatation, systolic dysfunction, apical aneurysm formation, and heart failure, with mural thrombi predisposing to systemic embolism.
additionalInvestigations: Serological testing for Trypanosoma cruzi antibodies, typically using more than one assay
12-lead ECG for conduction abnormalities and arrhythmia
Echocardiography for ventricular function and apical aneurysm
Ambulatory monitoring for ventricular arrhythmia and conduction block
Cardiac MRI for fibrosis and regional dysfunction where available
Assessment of thromboembolic risk and evaluation for gastrointestinal involvement
redFlags: High-grade atrioventricular block or symptomatic bradycardia
Sustained ventricular tachycardia or aborted sudden cardiac death
Progressive heart failure with severely impaired function
Systemic embolism from an apical aneurysm or mural thrombus
reference.prognosis: The indeterminate phase carries a good prognosis, but once cardiomyopathy develops the outlook worsens with the degree of ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmic burden, and heart failure severity. Sudden cardiac death, progressive heart failure, and thromboembolism are the principal causes of mortality; risk stratification guides device therapy and anticoagulation.
pitfalls: Not asking about origin from or travel to endemic regions in unexplained cardiomyopathy
Overlooking conduction disease and arrhythmic risk that can cause sudden death
Missing an apical aneurysm and its associated thromboembolic risk
Assuming antiparasitic treatment will reverse established structural heart disease
Failing to consider associated gastrointestinal (megaoesophagus, megacolon) disease
management: Give guideline-directed heart failure therapy with beta-blockers, ACE inhibitors or angiotensin receptor blockers, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists and diuretics for systolic dysfunction
Consider antitrypanosomal therapy with benznidazole or nifurtimox, recognising its limited benefit once established cardiomyopathy is present but its greater role in earlier disease
Manage bradyarrhythmia and conduction disease with pacing, and reduce sudden-death risk with amiodarone and an implantable cardioverter-defibrillator in selected patients
Anticoagulate patients with apical aneurysm, mural thrombus, atrial fibrillation or prior embolism to prevent systemic thromboembolism
Monitor with periodic electrocardiography, ambulatory rhythm monitoring and echocardiography to track ventricular function and arrhythmic burden
Consider catheter ablation for refractory ventricular tachycardia and advanced options such as cardiac transplantation in end-stage heart failure
Screen family members and blood and organ donors, and evaluate for coexisting gastrointestinal involvement such as mega-oesophagus and megacolon
